Oncology / Cancer supportive care · published research

HSCT-induced taste changes

In an 85-person sham-controlled trial after hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, tongue PBM reduced taste dysfunction during severe neutropenia and engraftment and helped prevent lingual papilla atrophy.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In an 85-person sham-controlled trial after hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, tongue PBM reduced taste dysfunction during severe neutropenia and engraftment and helped prevent lingual papilla atrophy.

Summary of the Evidence

One unique human randomized sham-controlled trial studied taste changes after hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation. It enrolled 85 patients, with 42 assigned to PBM and 43 to placebo. No second publication or independent patient cohort, animal study, or standalone laboratory experiment was identified for this indication.

Human and clinical evidence

Ferreira and colleagues reported less hypogeusia, ageusia, and parageusia in the PBM group at severe neutropenia and engraftment, and prevention of lingual papilla atrophy. These findings concern taste outcomes during the transplant course; they do not establish persistence after engraftment or effects on nutritional status. The paper is a randomized placebo-controlled trial, but it remains one study and needs independent confirmation (Ferreira et al. 2024).

Animal evidence

No relevant animal study was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell, tissue, or laboratory study was identified. Papilla measurements were clinical outcomes in transplant recipients.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The trial used an InGaAlP red laser at 660 nm, with reported power of 100 mW, irradiance of 1.1 W/cm², and fluence of 8.8 J/cm² on the dorsum of the tongue. These parameters describe a localized oral protocol in transplant recipients and should not be assumed to apply to other causes of taste change or other PBM devices.

Interpretation

The randomized comparison supports a short-term reduction in several taste disturbances during transplant recovery. Persistence, functional importance, and reproducibility remain uncertain because the evidence is one clinical trial.

Evidence strength in source summaryTaste dysfunction during severe neutropenia and engraftment: Low
Publications and records1 unique title

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One randomized sham-controlled trial in 85 transplant recipients reported reduced hypogeusia, ageusia, and parageusia at important treatment time points. This is direct evidence but comes from one cohort and needs independent replication. Longer follow-up should establish whether effects persist after engraftment and improve eating or nutritional outcomes.
